draft.title: Depreciation
card: A non-current asset, such as a delivery van, is used by a business for more than one year. It helps earn revenue over many years.
Depreciation spreads the cost of the asset as an expense over its useful life. Useful life is the time the business expects to use the asset.
Assets lose value because they wear out from use or become obsolete. Obsolete means out of date, for example when newer equipment does the job better.
Depreciation matches the cost to the years in which the asset helps earn revenue. It is not a cash payment, and it is not the cost of repairs.
draft.remember: Depreciation shares an asset's cost across the years it is used, instead of expensing it all at once.

a.q: Why does a business record depreciation on a non-current asset?
opts: To spread the asset's cost over the years it is used
To save cash for buying a new asset when it is needed
To record the cost of repairing the asset each year
To show what the asset could be sold for each year
a.why: Depreciation matches the cost of the asset to the years in which it helps earn revenue. It is not a cash saving or a repair cost, because it is an expense recorded without any payment being made.
a.clue: Think about when the asset helps earn revenue.

b.q: Jess's bakery in Ballarat buys an oven for $12,000 and expects to use it for six years. How should the cost of the oven be treated?
opts: Spread as a depreciation expense over the six years
Recorded as an expense in full in the year it is bought
Recorded as an expense only in the year the oven is sold
Spread as a repair expense over the six years
b.why: The oven helps earn revenue for six years, so its cost is spread as depreciation over that time. Expensing it all in year one would put the whole cost in one year, even though the oven is used in all six.
b.clue: The oven is used for more than one year.

a.best: To spread the asset's cost over the years it is used

b.best: Spread as a depreciation expense over the six years
